record.paper_title: A survey of open questions in adaptive therapy: bridging mathematics and clinical translation
record.original_question: What adaptive dose administration protocol best balances tumor control, resistance delay, toxicity, clinical feasibility, and empirical robustness? In adaptive cancer therapy, should dosing use dose skipping or dose modulation; should tumor size be held near a maximal acceptable threshold to maximize competitive suppression; when should treatment switch to maximum tolerated dose if resistant cells are partially resistant; how should stabilization doses and dose titration be chosen; and how should protocols respond to tumor size changes, spatial structure, cell mobility, quiescence, and other phenomena that simple models may miss?

evidence.quote: 2.2 What is the optimal adaptive dose administration protocol?

Many models emphasize competition between sensitive and highly resistant cells and assume that the larger the tumor size, the stronger the competition [70, 57, 2, 67, 71, 72, 32, 25]. Such models suggest maintaining the tumor at the maximal acceptable size, in order to maximize competitive suppression of resistance [63, 25].

The switching time could be timed with a decrease of treatment efficiency [73], but the practical implementation and whether similar conclusions hold for models with many types of tumor cells [76] remains to be investigated.
A practical question is to determine the appropriate stabilization dose.
This highlights that simple models may miss important phenomena and that more data and modeling are needed to optimize adaptive therapies.

artifact.status_search_result: This is an explicitly posed open research question in a survey on adaptive cancer therapy. No single protocol has been established as optimal: ongoing modeling and clinical-trial work (e.g. adaptive abiraterone trials and follow-up theoretical studies) continues to compare dose-skipping vs dose-modulation and to explore titration, switching times, and spatially structured models, without a definitive resolution.
